en: The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra. [Posthumous title of the translator:
Duke of Sui, with a fief of three thousand households; Grand Master of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial;
conferred the purple robe and the rank of Minister of Works; posthumously titled Dajian (Great Mirror). Zhenghao (Correct Title).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, Śramaṇa of Great and Vast Wisdom at Daxingshan Temple, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the House of Mṛgāramātṛ, within the great multi-storied pavilion of Sandalwood Treasury, having attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
Ten years hence, at the time of the summer heat, he will be accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus—
śrāvakas, both those still in training and those beyond training, arhats whose outflows are exhausted and who are free from further afflictions,
all having attained mastery, with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated, having obtained right knowledge.
They were like great dragons who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit,
exhausted all fetters of existence, and reached the further shore— namely, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, and the Venerable Gayākāśyapa.
Kāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Kuṭhila,
the Venerable Bakula, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
the Venerable Vāgīśvara, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Venerable Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable Udāyin, the Venerable Rāhula, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Upānanda, the Venerable Ānanda,
and one thousand other bhikṣus headed by these as their leaders were all present together.

Furthermore, there were sixty *gaṅgā*-river-sands of *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* who had gathered together from various buddha-fields—all of whom were in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), possessed great supernormal powers, strengths, and fearlessnesses, and had already served countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas; all were capable of turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma;

and such that if sentient beings in immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds merely uttered their names, they would all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They were as follows: the *bodhisattva* Dharmamati...
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati, the Bodhisattva Vyāghramati, the Bodhisattva Arthamati, the Bodhisattva Jitamati,
the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Ratnacandraprabha, the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandraprabha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya, the Bodhisattva Aparimitavīrya, the Bodhisattva Anantavīrya, and the [Bodhisattvas of] the Three Times.
The Bodhisattva Vīrakrama, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin,
the Bodhisattva Gandhasugandha, the Bodhisattva Gandhasugandhaśrī, the Bodhisattva Śrīgarbha, the Bodhisattva Ketu,
the Bodhisattva Mahādhvaja, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, and the Bodhisattva Anuttaradhvaja.
Sāgarabuddhi Bodhisattva, Ratnakṣetrapratividdha Bodhisattva, Vimalaratnakṣetra Bodhisattva,
Nandirāja Bodhisattva, Nityananda Bodhisattva, Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, Meru Bodhisattva, Mahāmeru Bodhisattva,
Sumeru Bodhisattva, Guṇaratnaprabhāsa Bodhisattva, Dhāra... [Bodhisattva]...
The Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Nis, the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder, the Bodhisattva Who Eliminates the Illnesses of All Sentient Beings,
the Bodhisattva Joyful Mind, the Bodhisattva Sorrowful Mind, the Bodhisattva Free from Sorrow,
the Bodhisattva Treasury of Light, the Bodhisattva Sandalwood, the Bodhisattva Without Strife Herein, and the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Thunder-Sound.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarva, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bodhicaryārambha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvadharmeśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta— headed by these and others— were accompanied by sixty *gaṅgā*-sands of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, from immeasurable worlds, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others all came to assemble;
additionally, kings, ministers, officials, elders, householders, and various multitudes of people all came to assemble.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a multitude of hundreds of thousands who paid him respect and made offerings.

Then, after the meal, while within the Great Pavilion of Sandalwood Treasury, the World-Honored One entered the power of the Buddha's spiritual authority; consequently, from the Sandalwood Treasury, there suddenly emerged hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of lotus flowers. Each lotus flower had hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of petals, their size like chariot wheels, and they were endowed with perfect color and fragrance.
These lotuses ascended into the void, completely covering all buddha-fields; they joined together to form a single jewel palace that remained suspended in space.

All those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotuses were in full bloom; within each and every flower sat a Tathāgata in the full lotus posture, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light.

At that time, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the petals of all the lotuses suddenly withered and shriveled; their color and form became foul-smelling and loathsome, such that none were pleasing to the mind.

From within the calyxes of the flowers, the various Tathāgatas each emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light, universally manifesting all the buddha-fields, all of which were perfectly adorned and majestic.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly were utterly astonished and gave rise to a sense of wonder, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had manifested such supernatural feats, the great multitude, seeing this, all harbored doubts and reflected:

"By what causes and conditions have these hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotuses appeared, only to have their colors and forms deteriorate in an instant until they become utterly loathsome and no longer pleasing?"

“Within the lotus, the form of a Tathāgata appears, sitting in the full lotus posture and emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light; how is it that such light causes people to feel love and joy?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajramati and the entire great assembly all gathered together within the Great Pavilion of Sandalwood Treasury and sat respectfully.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajramati, saying:
"O son of good family!
You should now question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound essentials of the Dharma."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramati, receiving the holy intent of the Buddha, spoke to the Buddha for the sake of all devas, humans, and the world, as well as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly who harbored doubts, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

By what causes and conditions do hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotuses appear throughout all worlds, with a Tathāgata seated cross-legged within the calyx of every flower emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light;

and why do these lotuses suddenly become so loathsome in form and color as to inspire revulsion, while those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas within them remain standing with palms joined, solemnly unmoving?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramati asked in verse:
"I have never before seen the Tathāgata manifest such supernatural transformations;
He displays thousands of millions of Buddhas, yet remains motionless within the womb of the lotus."
Emitting a thousand rays of light that manifest as reflections, they completely outshine all buddha-fields;
sporting with marvelous skill in the Dharma, those Buddhas are all perfectly dignified and majestic.
Appearing like a wondrous jewel, you sit upon a lotus of foul color;
since every petal of this lotus is loathsome, how is it that you perform such great supernormal powers?
I have seen Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and witnessed their supreme miraculous feats;
yet I have never before seen such a sign as this, so manifest in your present play.
I pray that the Honored One among Gods will explain: by what cause and by what condition has this appeared?
I pray that the Benefactor of the World will show compassion, so as to dispel all doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the leading Bodhisattvas, such as Vajramati, and all the assembly of Bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
There is a profound essential teaching entitled the *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* which the Tathāgata wishes to expound; for this reason, he has first manifested such physical signs."
"Listen well, listen very well, and attend with focused attention!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajramati and all the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas said:
"Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“O sons of good family!

These lotus flowers manifested by the Tathāgata suddenly assume a foul appearance—malodorous, loathsome, and unpleasant to behold—and yet within these flowers appear the forms of Buddhas, sitting cross-legged and emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light, their marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) so dignified and majestic that all people delight in seeing them.”
Having known this, many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others paid homage and made offerings.
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the light of his own buddha-wisdom, perceives with his eye all sentient beings' desire, hatred, delusion, greed, ignorance, and afflictions."
Those sons and daughters of good family are overwhelmed and submerged by afflictions; yet within their wombs there are hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, all of whom are exactly like me.

With the eye of Tathāgata-wisdom, he observes that those beings possess the essence of the Buddha-dharma; sitting cross-legged in silent immobility, amidst all the defilements of affliction, the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata is fundamentally unshakable and cannot be stained by any views regarding the realms of existence.
Therefore, I now speak these words:
"All those Tathāgatas are no different from me.
O son of good family!
In this way, the Tathāgata, with the eye of Buddha-wisdom, perceives the *tathāgatagarbha* within all sentient beings.
Son of good family!

It is like using the sublime celestial eye to see such foul colors and foul odors, where [the Buddha] is enveloped and constrained by the petals of various lotuses; thus, with the divine eye, one sees within those flowers the true body of the Buddha sitting in the full lotus posture.
Having understood this, those who wish to see the Tathāgata must eliminate their foul and impure evil karma, in order to manifest the physical form and marks of the Buddha. It is so, it is so!
"Good son!

With the Buddha-eye, the Tathāgata observes the tathāgatagarbha within all sentient beings; he preaches the Dharma for them so that their store of desire, hatred, delusion, greed, ignorance, and afflictions may be entirely eliminated.
By hearing this Dharma, they practice correctly and thereby attain the pure, true essence of the Tathāgata."
"Good son!

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the tathāgatagarbha of all sentient beings are eternally constant and unchanging."
"Furthermore, noble son!

If there are sentient beings who are bound by the storehouse of loathsome afflictions, for the sake of eliminating and destroying that storehouse of afflictions and purifying the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaches the essential points of the Dharma to bodhisattvas, performing such deeds to inspire their resolute understanding."
Having gained such conviction, one maintains firm adherence to the Dharma and thereby attains liberation from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is counted among those in the world who are capable of performing the Buddha-work of a Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as that lotus flower is loathsome, Along with its sheath, leaves, stamens, and filaments,
If one were to behold it with the divine eye, One would see that this Tathāgatagarbha is unstained."
If one can remove the withered flowers and leaves, One will immediately behold the Tathāgata’s body within;
Furthermore, being unstained by the various afflictions, One shall attain perfect enlightenment within the world.
Now I see that within all sentient beings there exists the subtle and wondrous body of a Tathāgata;
having removed their thousands of millions of afflictions, I cause them to loathe them as one would a withered lotus.
I dispel [their suffering] for their sake; I, the wise one, constantly proclaim the sublime Dharma.
The Buddha always keeps those sentient beings in mind, wishing that they all may attain the very body of a Tathāgata.
With my Buddha-eye I behold that all sentient beings abide in the state of Buddhahood;
therefore, I constantly preach the sublime Dharma so that they may attain the three bodies and possess Buddha-wisdom.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a honeycomb suspended from a great tree, round in shape, guarded by hundreds of thousands of bees. A man seeking honey uses skillful means to drive away the bees and take the honey for whatever purpose it may serve."

"So it is, so it is! Son of good family, all sentient beings are like a honeycomb, guarded and protected by hundreds of thousands of millions of afflictions and secondary afflictions. When one has come to know this through the wisdom and vision of a Buddha, one then attains perfect enlightenment."
"Good son!
Just as a wise man, having recognized honey in such a hive, also understands that it is guarded by hundreds of thousands of millions of bees of affliction;

so too, all sentient beings have already attained Buddhahood through the Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision, yet they are obscured by hundreds of thousands of millions of afflictions and secondary afflictions."
"Good son!

With skillful means, the Tathāgata acts as one who harms bees for the sake of sentient beings; he teaches them to drive away desire, hatred, ignorance, pride, arrogance, concealment, anger, rage, envy, stinginess, afflictions, and secondary afflictions. Thus he preaches the Dharma, so that sentient beings are not defiled by afflictions, nor further oppressed by them, nor do they remain in their proximity."
"Good son!
How is it that for the sake of purifying these sentient beings through the Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision, I perform buddha-work within all worlds?"
“Good son!
With the pure eye, one sees all sentient beings as thus pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a honeycomb, round in shape, is guarded and concealed by a swarm of bees,
when a man seeking honey sees it, he drives away all those bees."
I see sentient beings within the three realms of existence as being no different from a honeycomb;
amidst the bees of affliction of millions of beings, the Tathāgata dwells within those very afflictions.
Because our Buddha constantly purifies and removes them, he destroys those afflictions like driving away bees;
through skillful means he preaches the Dharma, causing billions of sentient beings to destroy their manifold afflictions.
How does one attain Buddhahood and perform the Buddha-work?
Constantly appearing in the world like a vessel of honey, speaking of exquisite honey with eloquence, one causes others to realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like rice, wheat, millet, and beans; their essential core is enveloped by husks, and if the husks are not removed, they are unfit for consumption."
"Good son!
Whether they be men or women, those who seek food use mortars and pestles to pound away the husks so as to provide themselves with nourishment. It is even so; it is even so!"
"Good son!

With the Tathāgata-eye, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha perceives that all sentient beings possess the essence of a Tathāgata, yet it is enveloped by the skin of afflictions. If they can awaken to this understanding, they will achieve perfect enlightenment and dwell firmly in spontaneous wisdom."
"Good son!

That Tathāgatagarbha dwells amidst all afflictions; for the sake of those sentient beings, the Tathāgata removes the skin of their afflictions, causing them to become pure and attain Buddhahood. He teaches the Dharma for them, constantly thinking:
'When will these sentient beings cast off the skin of the storehouse of all afflictions and succeed in becoming Tathāgatas appearing in the world?'"
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Just as rice, millet, and wild grain, Or wheat, barley, and various beans—
When they are enveloped by their husks, They are unfit for consumption."
If one can use the pestle to husk away the chaff, the various grains will be fit for consumption;
yet the kernel within the husk is unfit [if left unhusked]. Likewise, one should not harm sentient beings, but act for their benefit.
I constantly observe all sentient beings, whose Tathāgata-wisdom is wrapped within afflictions;
for their sake, I preach the sublime Dharma to remove the husks, wishing that they may swiftly awaken and realize Bodhi.
For all sentient beings who share my Dharma, yet dwell enveloped within a hundred afflictions, I preach the Dharma so that they may purify them;
when will they swiftly attain the body of a Buddha?
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a heap of foul and putrid filth, through which a man carrying a gold brick passes by. Suddenly, he mistakenly drops it into the filth.

This precious gold sinks into the stench and remains there amidst the excrement for ten years, twenty years, fifty years, or even hundreds of thousands of years. Yet its essential nature remains neither destroyed nor defiled; however, it likewise cannot provide any benefit to people."
"Good son!
One who possesses the divine eye sees those gold bricks amidst the filth and stench and says to others: 'O man!'"
"There is a superior treasure of gold within that filth and excrement; go there.
Having heard this, the man took it, washed it clean once he had obtained it, and used the gold for its intended purposes.
"Good son!
That which is a heap of foul impurities is called the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
those golden bricks are called the indestructible dharma."
One who possesses the divine eye is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Son of good family!

The *dharmatā* of all sentient beings is a truly supreme jewel, yet it is submerged within the foul impurities of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in order to remove for sentient beings the foul impurities and impurity of the afflictions, preaches the sublime Dharma so that they may attain Buddhahood; he appears in the world and performs the work of a Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as if a person were carrying a gold brick, And suddenly, by mistake, dropped it into filth;
Though it remained within that impurity for many years, Despite the long passage of time, it would not decay."
One who possesses the divine eye beholds this and says to others:
"There is gold here; you should take it, wash it, and use it as you please.
Immersed in the long night of the flowing stream of afflictions and impurities, one knows that those afflictions are but adventitious dust.
"Through the skillful means of teaching intrinsic purity, one is led to realize the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, son of good family,
it is like a poor man whose house contains a great hidden treasure beneath the floor, measuring exactly one krośa in length and breadth, filled with abundant gold."
That gold lies at a depth of seventy cubits; because it is covered by the earth, that great treasury of gold has never spoken a word to that man, saying: "O man!"
"I am here; I am called the Great Treasure.

Yet that impoverished man, harboring feelings of destitution and suffering from grief and distress, ponders this day and night as he moves back and forth above it, completely unaware, neither hearing nor seeing that great treasure hidden within the earth.
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family,

all sentient beings dwell within the house of grasping at mental attention, yet they possess the treasury of the Tathāgata’s dharmas— the wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses— while they suffer by being attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles."
Because of this, one does not hear the great treasury of the Dharma-jewels, much less obtain anything from it.
If those five desires are extinguished, then one attains purity.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he reveals various treasuries of the Great Dharma amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas;
having gained resolute conviction therein, they then dig and excavate, entering the abodes of bodhisattvas.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the treasury of the Dharma for the world; seeing the unprecedented causal signs within all sentient beings, he therefore employs parables to expound the great treasury of the Dharma. He is the great donor of the treasury of unimpeded eloquence, immeasurable wisdom, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
In this way, son of good family!
With his pure eye, the Tathāgata perceives that all sentient beings possess the tathāgatagarbha; it is for this reason that he proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as in the house of a poor man there is a hidden treasure, Filled with gold and jewels within;
It remains unmoving and without thought, And it does not say of itself, 'I am such-and-such a thing.'"
Although that person is once again a sovereign, they experience poverty without realizing it;
they do not speak of it to others, yet they endure poverty while dwelling in suffering.
Thus, with my Buddha-eye I observe that all sentient beings, though dwelling in poverty and deprivation,
possess within their bodies a great hidden treasury, abiding as the essence of all Buddhas, unshakable.
Beholding their essence, he spoke to the bodhisattvas:
"You shall pierce this treasury of great wisdom, thereby attaining freedom from poverty and becoming World-Honored Ones, able to bestow the supreme wealth of the Dharma."
I have explained that all sentient beings possess a hidden treasure;
if one can resolve with conviction and apply diligent effort, one will swiftly realize supreme enlightenment.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like the seeds of the rattan, the tāla, the jambu, and the āmalaka; because their sprouts develop and transform one after another, they constitute an indestructible dharma. If they encounter the condition of earth and are planted, after a long time they will become great king-trees."

"So it is, so it is! Son of good family, with the Tathāgata-eye, the Tathāgata sees that within all sentient beings—down to the very limits of their skin—there exist desire, hatred, delusion, greed, ignorance, and afflictions; yet within this treasury of desire, hatred, delusion, ignorance, and afflictions, there is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. For this reason, it is called 'possessing the nature'."
If one can bring cessation to rest, it is called "coolness," and is thus termed *nirvāṇa*.

If one can purify and eliminate ignorance and afflictions, that realm of sentient beings is termed the "essence of the mass of great wisdom," and those sentient beings are called the "mass of great wisdom."
If a Buddha appears in the world of devas and preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma, one who perceives this is called a Tathāgata.
Son of good family!
If they perceive the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, it is so that all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may fully awaken to and understand the wisdom of the Tathāgata, causing it to be manifested.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as trees are found within the seeds of the *vetra* vine, and every sprout of the vine can be obtained;
so too, throughout the entire Jambudvīpa, they all exist because they have been planted and thus are able to grow."
Thus, this view of mine is entirely without remainder: all sentient beings are like the seeds of a vine;
when observed with the supreme, untainted Buddha-eye, the essence of the Tathāgata is fully present within them.
That which is indestructible is called the "store" (garbha) of sentient beings; within it, wisdom is non-different [from its object].
Abiding peacefully in the state of meditative concentration, it is also unshakable and without anything to be attained.
I preach the Dharma for their purification: how may these beings attain perfect enlightenment?
Just as a seed grows into a great tree, they shall become the refuge of the world.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a poor man who fashions an image of the Tathāgata out of all kinds of jewels, measuring one cubit in height.

This poor man, wishing to carry the jeweled image across a perilous road, fears it will be stolen or plundered; he therefore takes foul-smelling, filthy, and tattered rags to wrap around the image so that no one may discern it."
"Good son!

This impoverished man died suddenly in the wilderness; meanwhile, the precious image of the Tathāgata lay within foul-smelling, tattered rags, cast upon the ground and left to drift in the wilderness.
As people traveling along the road passed back and forth, they trampled and leaped over it, unaware that the form of the Tathāgata was within."
Because he was wrapped in foul and filthy cloth and cast upon the ground, everyone felt revulsion toward him; how could they have conceived the thought that he was a Buddha?
At that time, the devas dwelling in the wilderness saw this with their divine eyes and immediately addressed the other people traveling along the road, saying:
"O noble sirs!..."
"Within these foul rags is an image of the Tathāgata; it should be quickly uncovered, for all the world ought to pay it homage and respect. "So it is, so it is!"
"Good son!

With the Tathāgata-eye, the Tathāgata sees that all sentient beings are like those foul and putrid rags of affliction, wandering through the long, perilous wilderness of saṃsāra, and undergoing immeasurable bodies among the animals."
Within the tattered rags of the defilements of all sentient beings, there exists the body of a Tathāgata, no different from my own;
because the Tathāgata seeks to untie the wrappings of these defiled rags of affliction, he preaches the sublime Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas:
"How may you attain the pure wisdom and vision of a Tathāgata, depart from afflictions, and receive the veneration of all the world, just as I do?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a foul cloth causes loathing, So it was wrapped around the body of that Tathāgata.
A precious image shrouded in filthy rags Was cast away in a desolate and treacherous wilderness."
Having seen it with their divine eyes, the devas immediately said to the other people on the road:
"A precious image is within that foul cloth; you should quickly unwrap it and pay it homage."
With my divine eye I see thus: I observe all sentient beings entangled in the silken cloth of afflictions, undergoing the extreme suffering of sorrow, distress, birth, and death.
Within the filthy rags of my afflictions, I see the body of the Tathāgata sitting in the full lotus posture;
dwelling in profound stillness, it is unmoving, for all things are non-existent—this is liberation.
Having seen that, you shall be startled into awakening; listen attentively and abide in supreme enlightenment!
Such is the nature of all sentient beings: within their very state of fear, the Buddha is ever-present.
Having thus liberated them, he manifests the body of a Buddha;
at that time, all afflictions are stilled, and for this reason he is named the Tathāgata, whom gods and humans joyfully honor.
"Furthermore, good son!

There may be a solitary woman who is misshapen, foul-smelling, and ugly in appearance, like a piśācī, whom people find loathsome and terrifying. She dwells in a lowly and wretched household; by chance she becomes pregnant through sexual intercourse, and it is certain that this is the womb of a Cakravartin king.
Nevertheless, although she is pregnant, she never entertains such thoughts; she harbors only a sense of poverty and inferiority, and because her mind is weak and base, she constantly thinks: "
"My form is ugly and deformed; I have spent my days dwelling in an inferior and wretched household, and I do not even know what kind of human being was born from my womb."

"So it is, so it is! Son of good family, all sentient beings are without master and without refuge; born within the three realms of existence, they dwell in inferior and wretched abodes, oppressed by the sufferings of birth and death."
Nevertheless, every single sentient being possesses the realm of the Tathāgata and is endowed with the Tathāgatagarbha; yet those beings do not perceive or know it.
Son of good family!
So that no sentient being may deceive themselves, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for them, saying:
"Good sons! Do not deceive yourselves;
arouse a mind of great and firm diligence. Within each of your bodies there exists the Buddha-nature, and in the future you shall all attain perfect enlightenment."
"You have now entered the ranks of the bodhisattvas and are thus no longer an ordinary person;
yet in the distant future, you will also fall into the ranks of the Tathāgatas and will thus no longer be a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a woman who has no protector, her appearance hideous and loathsome,
dwelling in a wretched, evil, and lowly household, might at some time conceive the fetus of a king."
Carrying such a fetus within her womb, she will certainly give birth to a Wheel-Turning King;
that monarch, surrounded by the majesty of the seven treasures, shall rule as sovereign over the four continents.
That foolish and ugly woman did not know at all that such a being was within her womb;
dwelling in a lowly, poor, and wretched house, she harbored the suffering of poverty and was tormented by grief and anxiety.
I see all sentient beings, who, being without a master, undergo the suffering of destitution;
though they dwell within the three realms, indulging in pleasures, the treasury of Dharma resides within their very bodies like a hidden embryo.
Having seen this, he addressed the Bodhisattva: "All sentient beings possess the *dharmatā*;
within the womb, there is the light of worldly benefit. You should give rise to reverence and not deceive."
By generating firm diligence in practice, one will before long become a Buddha oneself;
before long, one shall sit at the site of enlightenment and liberate immeasurable koṭis of beings.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like making a mold out of wax, either in the shape of a horse, an elephant, a man, or a woman, and covering its surface with clay. One then heats it with fire and melts refined gold to cast it into the mold. Once it has cooled, the craftsman takes it back to his home;

though the exterior of the mold is shrouded by black clay and its form appears scorched and ugly, there is a golden image within. When the craftsman or his apprentice realizes the mold has cooled, they break away the clay. Having cleaned it thoroughly, in a mere moment, this precious golden image becomes pure."
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family, with the Tathāgata’s eye,

the Tathāgata beholds all sentient beings as being like golden molds, externally enveloped by the mud of afflictions, yet within, empty and hollow, they are completely filled with the jewels of the Buddha-dharma’s untainted wisdom."
"Good son!

I now observe that all sentient beings are likewise thus; while I am preaching the sublime Dharma amidst this assembly of bodhisattvas, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains tranquility and coolness, the Tathāgata, for the sake of those sentient beings, purifies their Dharma-eye with the vajra weapon, removing their afflictions and secondary afflictions, in order to purify the treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-jewels."
"Good son! The Tathāgata is like one who holds a precious image; good son, he destroys that form along with its secondary afflictions, causing them to attain liberation—this is called the Tathāgata."
"O son of noble family!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, perceives that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha, yet it is submerged within a storehouse of boundless koṭis of afflictions. To enable those sentient beings to shatter the storehouse of afflictions and establish them in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment within the vision of Buddha-wisdom, [he teaches this Dharma]."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"Just as an external form made from clay serves as a mold, Its interior being empty and void of anything at all, One melts and refines pure gold and pours it into the cast; The number of such pieces may be a hundred or a thousand."
When the artisan knows it has cooled, he breaks through the clay to reveal the image;
once the clay is removed, the precious image is purified, and the artisan’s intent in carving and polishing is fully realized.
I see all sentient beings as golden images within clay molds;
though obscured from without by afflictions, the wisdom of the Tathāgata dwells within.
If one attains tranquility and coolness, the Bodhisattva of Pure Wisdom regarding the past strikes with the weapon of the Dharma-vessel, whereby all afflictions are utterly destroyed.
All the Buddha-sons of the Tathāgatas are as lovely as golden images;
they constantly receive offerings from devas and humans, possessing the marks of a perfected body and endowed with the ten powers.
I see all sentient beings thus purified and becoming Sugatas;
having achieved the state of a Sugata and attained the Buddha-eye, they fulfill unsurpassed sarvajñā.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vajramati, saying:

“Good son! If good sons or good daughters, whether lay or ordained, receive, uphold, read, recite, copy into volumes, and extensively explain to others this essential Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.”

There may be sons or daughters of good family, or other bodhisattvas, who, for the sake of accumulating the wisdom of the Tathāgatas, diligently make offerings to all Tathāgatas; in each and every world, they achieve such a form-samādhi (rūpa-samādhi).

By the power of this form-samādhi, they pass through Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and pay homage and serve Buddhas of the present as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and hundreds of billions of nayutas, as well as their assemblies of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the Saṅgha, at the abode of each and every Buddha.

In this manner, up until fifty *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, during times of harmonious and peaceful bliss, each sent forth hundreds of thousands of exquisite jeweled pavilions. Each was ten *yojana*s in height, and exactly one *yojana* in both length and breadth. All of these were made of precious materials and were celestial vessels of wondrous fragrance; they scattered various kinds of flowers and provided all manner of articles for enjoyment, continuing in this way day after day for as long as a thousand *kalpas*.

Vajramati! If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have resolved their minds toward awakening take even a single simile from this *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*—whether it be inscribed upon their own bodies or contained within a scroll.

Vajramati! Compared to this meritorious karma, the aforementioned meritorious karma—even when established by the Tathāgata as a hundredth part, a kāla-th part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a koṭi-th part, a hundred-koṭi-th part, a thousand-koṭi-th part, a hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part, or a hundred-thousand-nayuta-koṭi-th part—does not equal even a single kāla-th part of this; it is beyond reach even by calculation or analogy.

Vajramati! If there are sons or daughters of good family who seek unsurpassed enlightenment and, for a thousand kalpas, take hundreds of thousands of *manḍārava* flowers daily to offer as worship to those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the great assembly; and if they continue this for a full thousand kalpas—

Vajramati! If other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, having resolved their minds toward bodhicitta, hear this essential Dharma teaching of the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra, or even join their palms in reverent salutation and utter words of sympathetic joy; [they shall all attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].

Vajramati! By means of these superior roots of merit and goodness, compared with the merit of offering flowers from the previous roots of goodness, the Tathāgata establishes that the former merit does not equal even one part out of a hundred, a thousandth part, a millionth part, or an incalculable part of the latter.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Should there be those who joyfully seek awakening, Who, upon hearing this sutra, receive and uphold it,
Even to the point of transcribing it into volumes, And if they can show reverence for even a single stanza,"
One should listen to that merit, which is immeasurable, And give rise to an inexhaustible treasury of boundless virtue.
Having heard this Tathāgata-garbha Sūtra, If one can seek the practice for supreme bodhi,
Abiding in the Supreme Vehicle through supernormal powers, One shall offer worship and reverence to the Honored One among Men.
Together with the assembly of śrāvakas throughout the ten directions, even if they were to fulfill their practice for a thousand kalpas,
or many thousands of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would still surpass those inconceivable numbers.

In each world-system, there are immeasurable practices: exquisite pavilions made entirely of jewels, ten yojanas in height and one yojana in length and breadth, honored with ointments and burning incense;
within them are subtle seats of the seven precious gems.
With exquisite silks and brocades spread upon them, and other sublime seats likewise prepared,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River— one making offerings to each of the Buddhas and sending each to the abode of those Tathāgatas— [all] the Tathāgatas within every buddha-field.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges, all of whom he has honored and served.
Yet if a wise person hears this sutra and practices correctly by taking even a single metaphor from it,
or if they can receive, uphold, read, and recite it, the merit of this will surpass the previous mass of merit.
Sentient beings who take refuge in this sūtra will swiftly realize that unsurpassed enlightenment.
This Dharma corresponding to the Tathāgatagarbha— if a wise bodhisattva can contemplate it,
they will quickly awaken to the supreme dharmatā of all sentient beings and to spontaneous gnosis (svayambhū-jñāna).
The Buddha told Vajramati:
"By this you should know that such a Dharma-gate brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and is able to lead them to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*)."

Vajramati! I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable, incalculable, vast, inconceivable, and unspeakably infinite eons ago, at that time there was a Buddha named Constantly Emitting Radiance (Nityaprabhāsa), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Vajramati! For what reason and by what causes is that Blessed One named Constantly Emitting Radiance? Vajramati!

When that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Constantly Emitting Radiance (Sadāpramuktaraśmi), was a bodhisattva dwelling within his mother’s womb, the light from his body permeated outward, universally illuminating hundreds of thousands of worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields to the east;

having illuminated these, he likewise universally shone throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Vajramati! Because the Bodhisattva dwells within the mother’s womb, his bodily radiance shines universally throughout those worlds; this light brings people delight and gives rise to joy.

Vajramati! By the light radiating from the bodies of those bodhisattvas, hundreds of thousands of worlds as numerous as motes of dust are illuminated; the sentient beings therein who are touched by that light attain great majesty and are fully endowed with physical form, being possessed of mindfulness, wisdom, conduct, knowledge, and eloquence.

All sentient beings in those worlds who had fallen into the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, the world of Yama, or the asura destiny, were touched by the light radiating from that bodhisattva’s body; as soon as they were touched by that light, they all abandoned their bodies in the miserable destinies and were reborn among humans and devas.

All the humans and devas in those various worlds, through being touched by the light radiating from the Bodhisattva’s body, all attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi and acquired the five supernormal powers.

All the non-regressive bodhisattvas residing in those various worlds were touched by the light from the bodies of those bodhisattvas; as soon as that light touched them, they all attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and each obtained the *dhāraṇī* known as the "Five Hundredfold Merit Transformation."

In this way, hundreds of thousands of worlds as numerous as atoms were illuminated by the light from that bodhisattva’s body, becoming made of vaidūrya. Golden cords demarcated the eightfold paths, and rows of all kinds of jewel trees were arrayed in eight lines, adorned with flowers and fruits of extraordinary colors and fragrances.

As fragrant breezes shook those jewel trees, they produced harmonious, elegant, pleasing, and sublime sounds—namely, the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of the Saṅgha, the sound of the bodhisattvas, and the sound of enlightenment; as well as the sounds of the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, liberation, meditative concentrations, and attainments.
By the sound of the jewel trees, all sentient beings within hundreds of thousands of worlds as numerous as those atoms attained the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna.
All sentient beings within those worlds were freed from the realms of hell, the animal realm, the world of Yama, and the asura destinies.
While that Bodhisattva was within his mother’s womb, he remained with palms joined, radiant as the moon; throughout the six periods of day and night, he constantly emitted light until his birth.
Vajramati! That bodhisattva likewise attains perfect enlightenment immediately upon birth.
Once that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained Buddhahood, he constantly emits light from his body, continuing to emit light even until the time of his parinirvāṇa.
After that Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvāṇa, all his relics were enshrined within a stūpa, which constantly emitted radiance. Vajramati!
For this reason, the humans and devas of that time named that World-Honored One the Tathāgata Constantly Emitting Radiance.
"Furthermore, Vajramati!

During the time when that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Constantly Emitting Radiance, dwelt in the world, there was a bodhisattva named Immeasurable Light, who had a retinue of twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amitābha had already previously inquired about this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgatagarbha from that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Constantly Emitting Radiance.

Vajramati! That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Constantly Emitting Radiance remained seated upon his throne for five hundred kalpas, extensively proclaiming and expounding this *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*.

Through various phrases, he discerns the Dharma with unimpeded eloquence and hundreds of thousands of parables; out of compassion and to sustain those bodhisattvas, he extensively expounds this profound essential of the Tathāgatagarbha, so that in each of the worlds throughout the ten directions—numbering as many as the atoms within a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-fields—those bodhisattvas are all awakened by means of little effort.
Vajramati! Among them, those bodhisattvas who hear this *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, or even merely hear the title of this sūtra, will all gradually bring their roots of goodness to maturity.
Once they have matured, each will attain perfect enlightenment in a different land, with the exception of four bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not take up bodhi.
Vajramati! Do not harbor any other thought. At that time, was the Bodhisattva Amitābha anyone else?
It was none other than yourself.
Why is this? O Vajramati, in the past when you were a bodhisattva, your name was Amitaprabha. Vajramati!

In the time of that Buddha, those four bodhisattvas who did not take up enlightenment were the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and you, Vajramati, as the fourth.
Vajramati! Such is this essential Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha of great benefit; by hearing it, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve the wisdom of a Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One who constantly emitted radiance in the past, Throughout immeasurable kalpas of bygone ages,
Constantly emitted great light from his body, Illuminating hundreds of thousands of koṭis of worlds."

When he had first attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, at that time the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Light questioned that World-Honored One, the Dharma King: "How was this sūtra spoken at that time?"
During the time of that Buddha, they heard this sutra;
having heard it from that Buddha, they all attained supreme enlightenment, with the exception of these four bodhisattvas.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta and Avalokiteśvara, with Mañjuśrī as the third,
and you, Vajramati, as the fourth— on that occasion, you all heard this sutra.
The Bodhisattva Amitābha of former times was none other than you,
Vajramati; at that time, as a son of the Buddha,
you heard the name of this wondrous sutra from the presence of the Tathāgata Siṃhaketu.

Reverently joining my palms to hear this sutra, through these roots of goodness and karma from the past, I swiftly attained the state of supreme enlightenment; therefore, the wise should uphold this sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Vajramati, saying:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is bound by the fetters of karmic obstructions, and they hear this *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and expound it for others;

by virtue of hearing this scripture, reading and reciting it, receiving and upholding it, chanting it, expounding it, and transcribing its scrolls, their karmic obstructions will be extinguished with little effort, and the Buddha-dharma will manifest before them."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who are bound by the karmic obstacles of their entanglements, how many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, must they receive the empowerment of to preach the Dharma for them to attain extensive learning and become endowed with such essential teachings?"
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives empowerment and preaches the Dharma at the abodes of a hundred Buddhas—whether it be two hundred, or three, four, or five hundred; or a thousand, or two thousand; or three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten thousand Buddhas—at those places they preach the Dharma through empowerment.”

There are some who, at the abodes of two hundred thousand Buddhas, or even hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta Buddhas, have attained the power of dhāraṇī for retaining the teachings they hear. Ānanda!

If there is a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha, and copies it into a volume, recites it, receives and upholds it, contemplates its meaning, and explains it extensively for others, that bodhisattva should form this thought:
“I have now attained unsurpassed bodhi;
such a person should receive the offerings and respect of humans, devas, and asuras.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, they responded with joy. Then the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"When a bodhisattva hears this sūtra, they contemplate it and attain supreme awakening;
if anyone should obtain this scripture in their hands, humans and devas should pay homage and show them respect."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the Great Guides, praise that person as the foremost among men, and also call him the most excellent Dharma King.
This person shines like the full moon; he should receive veneration as does the World-Honored One.
"Capable of upholding the torch of the Dharma, he shall become a hero for the world, because this sutra has entered his hands.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajramati and the others, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas, humans, devas, asuras, and so forth, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra
